Heart: NKX2-5, TBX5, MEF2A/C, GATA4, HAND-related TFs indicate cardiac tissue
Reproductive/gonadal: AR, ESR1/2, NR5A1, DMRT1-3, SRY, RHOXF1/2 suggest gonadal tissue
cancer_cell_type_prediction_relevance: Leukemia/lymphoma: MYC, BCL6, RUNX1T1, ETV6, FLI1, ERG, NUP98 fusions, KMT2A rearrangements are hallmark oncogenes in hematologic malignancies
Prostate cancer: AR, NKX3-1, FOXA1 (absent but FOXA2 present), HOXB13 are key prostate cancer drivers
Breast cancer: ESR1, GATA3, FOXA2, RUNX2, YAP1, WWTR1 are relevant to breast cancer subtypes
Pediatric/developmental cancers: PAX3/7-FOXO1 fusions (rhabdomyosarcoma), EWS-FLI1 (EWSR1+FLI1 both present), NUP214 fusions suggest pediatric cancer relevance
Glioma/brain tumors: SOX2, OLIG2, IDH-related epigenetic TFs, FOXM1 are glioma markers
Pancreatic cancer: PDX1, GATA6, KLF5, MYC, KRAS-downstream TFs relevant to PDAC
cell_malignancy_status_prediction_releva: Malignant programs: MYC, TP53, CTCF, CREBBP/EP300 mutations are among the most common cancer alterations; their expression patterns can distinguish malignant from normal
EMT markers: SNAI1/2, ZEB1/2, TWIST-related, FOXC1/2 are canonical EMT TFs marking invasive/malignant states
Stemness: NANOG, POU5F1, SOX2, PRDM14 mark cancer stem cell programs associated with malignancy
Epigenetic dysregulation: KMT2A/C/D, ARID1A/B, BCOR, ASXL2/3 are frequently mutated tumor suppressors; loss-of-function marks malignant cells
Cell cycle deregulation: E2F1-5/7/8, MYBL2, FOXM1, MYC, LATS1 are proliferation/malignancy markers
drug_sensitivity_relevance: AR antagonists (enzalutamide, abiraterone): AR expression central to prostate cancer drug response
ESR1 modulators (tamoxifen, fulvestrant): ESR1 status determines hormone receptor-positive breast cancer treatment
BET bromodomain inhibitors (JQ1, OTX015): MYC, BCL6, FOSL1 transcriptional programs are BET-dependent
HDAC inhibitors (vorinostat, romidepsin): HDAC4/5/7/9, SIN3A, NCOR1 co-repressor complexes are direct targets
KMT2A/MLL inhibitors (menin inhibitors): KMT2A, MEIS1, HOXA9 leukemia program is targetable by menin-MLL inhibitors
CDK12 inhibitors: CDK12 present; relevant to BRCA-like cancers and immunotherapy response
PARP inhibitors: TP53, BRCA-pathway TFs relevant to HR-deficient tumors
Retinoic acid/RAR agonists: RARA, RARB, RARG, RXRA/B/G, NR2F1/2 mediate retinoid sensitivity in AML and other cancers
perturbation_modeling_relevance: Master regulator perturbations: Many TFs here (GATA1, PAX5, CEBPA, NANOG, SOX2) are classical master regulators whose perturbation causes large transcriptional cascades—ideal GEARS/CPA targets
Epistasis/GI mapping: Extensive TF family paralogs (KLF, FOX, SOX, HOX, GATA) enable systematic genetic interaction screens for redundancy and compensation
Chromatin remodeler KOs: ARID1A, CHD7/8, KMT2A/C/D, CREBBP/EP300 perturbations model epigenetic reprogramming
Fusion oncogene modeling: NUP98, EWSR1, ETV6, RUNX1T1 fusion partners present—relevant to modeling chromosomal translocation effects
Cell fate reprogramming: POU5F1, SOX2, KLF4, MYC (Yamanaka factors all present) are canonical reprogramming perturbation targets
Circadian perturbations: CLOCK, PER1-3, NR1D1/2 enable modeling of circadian disruption effects on gene expression
qc_warnings: Extremely large cluster (1101 genes): likely over-broad grouping of all transcriptional regulators rather than a functionally specific module

Mixed lineage TFs: cluster contains TFs from virtually every developmental lineage (neural, hematopoietic, endodermal, mesodermal) suggesting co-expression-independent grouping possibly based on GO annotation or protein domain similarity

Non-TF contaminants: NUP proteins (NUP98, NUP214, NUP153, NUP54, NUP58, NUP62), SEC proteins (SEC16A/B, SEC24C/D), RBM/CPEB RNA-binding proteins, BAG3/4 (chaperones), LATS1 (kinase), MAP2K4 (kinase), WNK1/2 (kinases), LGALS3 (lectin), COL17A1 (collagen) are functionally distinct from TFs
Housekeeping TFs mixed with tissue-specific: SP1, YY1AP1, TBP, GTF2A1, GTF3A are general transcription factors mixed with highly tissue-restricted TFs

Possible annotation-based clustering: The breadth suggests this cluster may reflect a gene ontology 'transcription factor activity' or 'DNA-binding' annotation pull rather than co-expression or co-regulation
Paralogs inflating cluster: Many gene families (39 HOX genes, 40+ FOX genes, 30+ ZNF/ZBTB genes) may be co-clustered due to sequence/domain similarity rather than functional co-expression
clusters.rationale: Cluster 7 contains 1101 genes that are overwhelmingly transcription factors and chromatin regulators spanning all major TF families. The representative gene BAZ2A is a chromatin reader/remodeler consistent with this theme. The cluster includes complete or near-complete representation of HOX, FOX, SOX, PAX, KLF, GATA, NR, ETS, bHLH, bZIP, ZNF, T-box, POU, NKX, DLX, IRX, CREB, MEF2, and TEAD families. This breadth strongly suggests the cluster was formed based on shared functional annotation (transcription factor/DNA-binding activity) or protein domain similarity rather than tight co-expression in a specific cell type. While internally coherent at the level of 'transcriptional regulation,' the cluster is too heterogeneous to represent a single biological program or cell state. Non-TF members (NUPs, kinases, RNA-binding proteins, a collagen) represent likely contamination or guilt-by-association clustering. The cluster has high utility for identifying transcriptional regulatory programs broadly but limited specificity for any single cell type or disease context without sub-clustering.
recommended_followups: Sub-cluster this large group using co-expression networks or protein-protein interaction data to identify functionally coherent modules (e.g., neural TFs, hematopoietic TFs, pluripotency TFs)
Remove non-TF members (NUPs, kinases, collagens, chaperones) and re-evaluate cluster coherence
Perform enrichment analysis against curated TF target gene sets (ENCODE ChIP-seq, JASPAR) to identify dominant regulatory programs
Test whether cluster members show coordinated expression in specific cell types using single-cell RNA-seq reference atlases (HCA, Tabula Sapiens)
Investigate NUP98, EWSR1, and KMT2A as fusion oncogene hubs within this cluster for cancer perturbation modeling
Apply SCENIC or similar TF activity inference to determine which TFs in this cluster are active regulators vs. merely expressed

clusters.title: Broad Cellular Housekeeping and Stress-Response Supercluster
clusters.overall_function: This large cluster encompasses a highly diverse set of genes spanning ubiquitin-proteasome system components, DNA damage response and repair, RNA processing, vesicular trafficking, mitochondrial function, lipid metabolism, protein quality control (ER stress/UPR), cell signaling (mTOR, TBK1, STK11/LKB1), autophagy, nucleocytoplasmic transport, and ciliogenesis. No single dominant pathway is evident; instead the cluster appears to aggregate broadly expressed housekeeping and stress-response genes.
cell_type_relevance: Non-specific: genes are broadly expressed across many cell types
Cycling/proliferating cells: DNA repair (ATM, FANCD2, MLH1, PRKDC), replication (POLA2, PRIM1, MCM9), and cell cycle (CCNE2, PRC1, STAG1) genes suggest relevance to proliferating states
Stressed/damaged cells: GADD45A/B, SESN1/2/3, HMOX1, CHAC1 indicate stress-response activation
Immune-relevant: TBK1, TNFAIP3, IRF1, IRAK3, MLKL, RIPK1 suggest innate immune signaling context
Autophagy-active cells: BECN1, ATG10, ATG13, EPG5, VMP1, WDFY3
cell_tissue_of_origin_prediction_relevan: Low specificity: the breadth of functions makes tissue-of-origin inference unreliable from this cluster alone
Possible enrichment in highly metabolically active tissues (liver, kidney, intestine) given lipid metabolism, peroxisomal, and mitochondrial genes
Ciliated epithelial tissues suggested by ciliogenesis genes (BBS4, BBS5, BBS10, BBS12, MKKS, CFAP46, CFAP54, ARL13B, CEP41)
Neuronal tissue hinted by NLGN1, NXPH1, NXPH4, GRIN2B, GPHN, MAP1B, but these may be noise in a large mixed cluster
cancer_cell_type_prediction_relevance: Tumor suppressor genes present (PTEN, TSC2, NF1, STK11, MLH1, ATM, BAP1, RB1CC1) suggest relevance to multiple cancer types with loss-of-function alterations
DNA damage response genes (FANCD2, FANCI, FANCC, PRKDC, XRCC5) relevant to genomically unstable cancers
mTOR pathway (MTOR, TSC2, RHEB, PTEN, STK11/STRADA) relevant to mTOR-driven cancers (renal, lung adenocarcinoma, endometrial)
Gasdermin family (GSDMA, GSDMB, GSDMC, GSDME) relevant to pyroptosis programs in cancer
Proliferation markers (CCNE2, PBK, FAM72A-D) relevant to high-grade malignancies
cell_malignancy_status_prediction_releva: Mixed signal: presence of tumor suppressors (PTEN, TSC2, NF1, MLH1) and DNA repair genes could mark non-malignant cells with intact checkpoints, or malignant cells with compensatory upregulation
Stress-response genes (SESN1/2/3, GADD45A/B, HMOX1) may be upregulated in both stressed normal and malignant cells
Autophagy genes (BECN1, ATG10/13) are context-dependent for malignancy
Overall: cluster is not a reliable standalone malignancy discriminator due to functional heterogeneity
drug_sensitivity_relevance: mTOR pathway (MTOR, TSC2, RHEB, STK11): sensitivity to rapalogs (everolimus, temsirolimus) and mTOR kinase inhibitors
TBK1: sensitivity to TBK1 inhibitors (e.g., MRT67307, BX795) relevant in KRAS-mutant cancers
PRKDC (DNA-PKcs): sensitivity to DNA-PK inhibitors (e.g., M3814/peposertib) in combination with DNA-damaging agents
ATM/FANC pathway: sensitivity to PARP inhibitors and platinum agents in HR-deficient contexts
PRMT5: sensitivity to PRMT5 inhibitors (e.g., GSK3326595) in MTAP-deleted tumors
USP7: sensitivity to USP7 inhibitors affecting p53 stabilization
TNFAIP3/RIPK1: relevance to TNF pathway inhibitors and necroptosis modulators
perturbation_modeling_relevance: TBK1 is a well-characterized perturbation target in innate immune and KRAS-synthetic lethality screens
MTOR, TSC2, PTEN, STK11 are canonical nodes for pathway perturbation modeling (PI3K/mTOR axis)
DNA repair genes (ATM, FANCD2, MLH1, PRKDC) are relevant for modeling genomic instability perturbations
CNOT1 (CCR4-NOT complex) and RNA processing genes relevant for post-transcriptional regulation perturbation
Large cluster size and functional heterogeneity limit precision of genetic interaction (GI) modeling; individual sub-pathway modules would be more tractable
Autophagy regulators (BECN1, ATG10, ATG13) are standard perturbation targets for autophagy flux studies
qc_warnings: Cluster is extremely large (1089 genes) with no coherent single biological function — strongly suggests over-aggregation or algorithmic artifact

Highly diverse functional categories co-clustered: ciliogenesis, DNA repair, lipid metabolism, innate immunity, mTOR signaling, RNA processing, vesicular trafficking — this breadth is atypical for a biologically meaningful co-expression or co-function cluster
Possible housekeeping gene contamination: many broadly expressed genes (ribosomal, translation factors, ubiquitin pathway) that co-cluster due to expression correlation rather than shared function
Presence of tissue-restricted genes (CASQ1/2 cardiac/muscle, GRIN2B neuronal, RYR3 muscle) alongside broadly expressed genes suggests mixed lineage contamination or batch effects
FAM72A/B/C/D paralogs and other gene family expansions may inflate cluster size artificially
Recommend sub-clustering or pathway enrichment analysis to identify coherent sub-modules
clusters.rationale: The cluster representative TBK1 is an innate immune kinase, but the 1089-member gene list spans an implausibly broad range of biological functions including ciliogenesis (BBS genes, CFAP genes), DNA repair (ATM, FANC genes, MLH1), mTOR signaling (MTOR, TSC2, PTEN, STK11), RNA processing (CNOT1, SF3A1, INTS genes), lipid metabolism (HADHA, MTTP, LCAT), ER quality control (PDIA2-6, TMX1-4, EDEM1), autophagy (BECN1, ATG10/13), and many transmembrane proteins of unknown function (TMEM genes). This diversity is inconsistent with a single coherent biological module. The cluster likely results from co-expression correlation across housekeeping and stress-response programs, possibly amplified by batch effects or overly permissive clustering parameters. Sub-pathway analysis is strongly recommended.
recommended_followups: Sub-cluster this group using stricter parameters (e.g., higher resolution Leiden/Louvain or hierarchical clustering) to identify coherent functional modules
Perform gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA/ORA) on sub-clusters to identify dominant pathways
Check for batch effect or technical covariation driving co-clustering of functionally unrelated genes
Examine expression correlation matrix within the cluster to identify hub genes vs. peripheral members
Assess whether tissue-restricted genes (CASQ1/2, GRIN2B, RYR3) are driving spurious co-clustering
Validate TBK1-centric innate immune sub-network by extracting TBK1, TNFAIP3, IRF1, IRAK3, MLKL, RIPK1 and their direct interactors as a separate module

clusters.title: KRAB-ZNF and Zinc Finger Transcription Factor Superfamily Cluster
clusters.overall_function: This cluster is dominated by Krüppel-associated box (KRAB) domain-containing zinc finger proteins (KRAB-ZNFs) and related zinc finger transcription factors, including ZNF, ZFP, ZKSCAN, ZSCAN, PRDM, and RBAK family members. These proteins primarily function as transcriptional repressors that recruit the KAP1/TRIM28 co-repressor and NuRD/SETDB1 complexes to silence transposable elements (TEs), retroviral sequences, and developmental genes. Additional members include PNMA family proteins (paraneoplastic antigens), RTL/PNMA-related retrotransposon-derived genes, PGBD1 (piggyBac transposable element derived), and MOAP1 (modulator of apoptosis). The cluster collectively represents a major arm of epigenetic and transcriptional regulation centered on TE silencing, genome defense, and developmental gene control.
cell_type_relevance: Germline and early embryonic cells: PRDM9 (meiotic recombination), ZFP57 (imprinting maintenance), ZSCAN4 (2-cell/totipotent state marker), ZFP42/REX1 (pluripotency), RTL1/RTL3-6 (retrotransposon-derived, placental/germline expression) suggest strong relevance to germ cells, early embryos, and pluripotent stem cells
Neurons and neural lineages: PNMA family proteins are paraneoplastic antigens expressed in neurons; cluster may mark neuronal or neuroendocrine cell states
Immune cells: MZF1 is a myeloid zinc finger expressed in myeloid progenitors; ZKSCAN3 has roles in autophagy regulation relevant to macrophages
Cycling/proliferating cells: Several KRAB-ZNFs are upregulated in proliferating contexts to suppress TE reactivation
cell_tissue_of_origin_prediction_relevan: Testis/germline: PRDM9, ZNF91, ZNF93, and many KRAB-ZNFs show highest expression in testis; cluster strongly suggests germline or gonadal tissue origin
Placenta/trophoblast: RTL1, RTL3-6 are retrotransposon-derived genes with known placental expression patterns
Brain/neural tissue: PNMA1, PNMA2, PNMA3, PNMA5, PNMA6A are paraneoplastic antigens with predominant neuronal expression
Embryonic/pluripotent: ZSCAN4, ZFP42 mark early embryonic or stem cell compartments
cancer_cell_type_prediction_relevance: Germ cell tumors (testicular cancer, ovarian germ cell tumors): High KRAB-ZNF and PRDM9 activity is characteristic of germ cell malignancies
Neuroendocrine tumors and paraneoplastic contexts: PNMA family proteins are classically upregulated in neuroendocrine cancers and trigger paraneoplastic neurological syndromes
Lung, colorectal, and other carcinomas: ZKSCAN3 has been reported as oncogenic in colorectal cancer; ZNF family members show altered expression across many carcinoma types
Melanoma and other cancers with TE reactivation: KRAB-ZNF silencing of TEs is relevant to cancers where TE reactivation drives immunogenicity or oncogene activation
cell_malignancy_status_prediction_releva: KRAB-ZNF repressors of TEs may distinguish malignant from normal cells if TE silencing is lost in cancer, potentially marking non-malignant or differentiated states
PNMA proteins are expressed in both normal neurons and certain tumor types, complicating malignancy discrimination
PRDM9 and ZSCAN4 expression in non-germline contexts may indicate aberrant epigenetic reprogramming associated with malignancy
Overall, this cluster is more informative for cell identity/lineage than binary malignancy status, though TE derepression signatures could serve as a malignancy indicator
drug_sensitivity_relevance: PRDM9 inhibition: relevant to cancers exploiting meiotic recombination programs; potential synthetic lethality targets

KRAB-ZNF/KAP1 axis: disruption of TRIM28 (KAP1) co-repressor interactions could sensitize cells to TE-driven innate immune activation (viral mimicry), potentially synergizing with immune checkpoint inhibitors
ZKSCAN3 inhibition: relevant to autophagy modulation and potential sensitivity to autophagy-targeting drugs in colorectal cancer
MOAP1 (MAOP): pro-apoptotic modulator; expression levels may influence sensitivity to apoptosis-inducing agents such as BH3 mimetics
Epigenetic drugs (HDAC inhibitors, DNMT inhibitors): likely to modulate expression of many KRAB-ZNFs and their TE targets, with downstream effects on immunogenicity
perturbation_modeling_relevance: KRAB-ZNF network is highly relevant for CRISPRi/CRISPRa perturbation screens targeting transcriptional repression of TEs and developmental genes
ZFP57 and PRDM9 perturbations are informative for modeling imprinting and meiotic recombination programs
ZSCAN4 perturbation is a key readout for 2C-like/totipotent state transitions in stem cell models
Genetic interaction (GI) screens: KRAB-ZNF paralogs show extensive redundancy, making GI mapping essential to understand epistasis within this large family
GEARS/perturbation prediction: the large size and paralog redundancy of this cluster make it a challenging but important test case for predicting combinatorial perturbation effects
RTL/PNMA retrotransposon-derived genes represent emerging perturbation targets for understanding domesticated TE function in development
qc_warnings: Cluster is very large (447 members), raising concern about over-lumping of functionally distinct KRAB-ZNF subfamilies that may have divergent regulatory targets
PNMA family proteins (paraneoplastic antigens) have distinct biological roles from canonical KRAB-ZNFs and may represent a functionally distinct sub-cluster
RTL/retrotransposon-derived genes (RTL1-6) and PGBD1 are structurally related to TEs but have been domesticated for host functions distinct from transcriptional repression
MOAP1 is a pro-apoptotic protein with no zinc finger domain; its inclusion warrants scrutiny

Fusion/readthrough gene symbols (e.g., ZNF625-ZNF20, ZNF670-ZNF695, RBAK-RBAKDN, ZNF286A-TBC1D26, ZNF816-ZNF321P) suggest possible annotation artifacts or readthrough transcripts that may not represent independent functional entities
ZKSCAN8P1 and ZNF722P are pseudogenes; their inclusion may indicate noise or co-expression with neighboring functional genes
The cluster likely reflects co-expression driven by shared chromosomal location (many ZNFs cluster on chromosomes 19 and X) rather than purely functional coherence
clusters.rationale: The vast majority of entities in this cluster are KRAB domain-containing zinc finger proteins (ZNF, ZFP, ZKSCAN, ZSCAN families) or closely related zinc finger transcription factors (PRDM, RBAK, ZIM, ZIK). These are well-established transcriptional repressors that co-evolved with transposable elements and function primarily through KAP1/TRIM28 recruitment. The cluster also contains PNMA family paraneoplastic antigens (which share structural similarity with retroviral Gag proteins and are expressed in neurons and certain tumors), RTL genes (retrotransposon-like, domesticated for placental and developmental functions), and a small number of outliers (MOAP1, PGBD1, SCAND1, WDR76). The co-clustering likely reflects shared expression patterns in germline/testis tissue, co-regulation by epigenetic machinery, and possibly genomic co-localization on ZNF-rich chromosomal regions. The cluster is biologically coherent at the broad level of 'zinc finger/TE-related transcriptional regulation' but contains functionally heterogeneous subgroups. The large size and inclusion of pseudogenes and fusion symbols are QC concerns.
recommended_followups: Sub-cluster the 447 members using finer resolution to separate canonical KRAB-ZNFs, PNMA/RTL retrotransposon-derived genes, ZSCAN/ZKSCAN subfamilies, and outliers (MOAP1, PGBD1)
Validate chromosomal co-localization as a driver of co-expression (check enrichment on chr19q, chrXq)
Cross-reference with ENCODE/GTEx tissue expression data to confirm testis/germline enrichment
Assess whether PNMA family members form a distinct sub-cluster with neuroendocrine expression
Remove or flag pseudogenes (ZKSCAN8P1, ZNF722P) and readthrough fusion symbols for downstream analyses
Perform GO enrichment and KRAB-domain annotation to quantify the fraction of bona fide KRAB-ZNFs vs. other zinc finger types
Investigate whether TE silencing activity (via TRIM28 ChIP-seq overlap) unifies the core cluster members
